title: Mean reversion: the Vasicek drift
objectives: Solve $dr/dt = \kappa(\theta - r)$ and read the half-life of a rate’s pull to its mean.

screens.title: A rate with a home
screens.prose: A short rate sits at 6%. It is pulled towards a long-run mean $\theta = 4\%$ at speed $\kappa$: $\dfrac{dr}{dt} = \kappa(\theta - r)$. Slide the start $r_0$ and the speed $\kappa$.
screens.question: What do all the paths have in common?

options.text: They all head to 4%, faster for larger $\kappa$

options.why: Try a start of 2%: the path rises. The pull is towards 4%, not 0.

options.text: Each settles near its own start
options.why: Move $r_0$ from 1% to 8%: every path ends at the dashed line.

options.text: Larger $\kappa$ moves the level they reach
options.why: $\kappa$ changes how fast, not where. The level is $\theta$.

feedback.correct: Every path ends at $\theta = 4\%$; $\kappa$ sets how fast.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try two starts and two speeds, and compare where each path ends.

explain.text: Above 4% the drift is negative and below it positive, so every path is pulled to $\theta$. This is **mean reversion**, the drift of the Vasicek model.

screens.title: Solve it either way
screens.prose: The gap $u = r - \theta$ obeys $u' = -\kappa u$, which separates (lesson 2): $u = u_0e^{-\kappa t}$. Or read $r' = -\kappa r + \kappa\theta$ as lesson 3's $y' = ay + q$, with steady level $\theta$. Both give $r(t) = \theta + (r_0 - \theta)e^{-\kappa t}$.
screens.question: With $r_0 = 6\%$, $\theta = 4\%$, $\kappa = 0.5$, what is $r(1)$, to 4 decimal places of a per cent?

hints.text: The gap at the start is 2 points.
After one year the gap is $0.02e^{-0.5} = 0.012131$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shrink the 2-point gap by $e^{-0.5}$, then add back 4%.

byKey.gap: You found the gap, 1.2131%, and forgot to add $\theta$ back.
byKey.decay: You shrank the whole rate, $6\% \times e^{-0.5}$. Only the gap to $\theta$ shrinks.

explain.text: $r(1) = 0.04 + 0.02e^{-0.5} = 5.2131\%$, and $r(2) = 0.04 + 0.02e^{-1} = 4.7358\%$. The gap shrinks by the same factor each year.

screens.title: The half-life
screens.prose: The gap halves in a fixed time, whatever its size: the **half-life**. Solve $e^{-\kappa t} = \tfrac12$. The dashed line at 5% marks a gap of half the start.
screens.question: With $\kappa = 0.5$, what is the half-life in years, to 4 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take logs of $e^{-0.5t} = \tfrac12$.

byKey.ln2: You found $\ln 2$ and stopped. Divide by $\kappa = 0.5$.
byKey.mean: $1/\kappa = 2$ is the time the gap falls to $1/e$ of its start, not to a half.

explain.text: $t_{1/2} = \ln 2/\kappa = 1.3863$ years. After one half-life the rate is 5%. After two, at 2.7726 years, it is 4.5%: a quarter of the gap is left.

screens.title: Speed from a half-life
screens.prose: Desks often quote the half-life and leave $\kappa$ implied. The relation runs both ways: $\kappa = \ln 2/t_{1/2}$.
screens.question: A model's half-life is 2 years. What is $\kappa$, to 4 decimal places?

byKey.recip: You took $1/t_{1/2}$. The factor $\ln 2$ belongs in it.

explain.text: $\kappa = \ln 2/2 = 0.3466$. A longer half-life means a smaller $\kappa$: the curve on the chart would flatten.

screens.title: The average rate over five years
screens.prose: A five-year loan pays the average rate: $\dfrac{1}{T}\int_0^T r\,dt = \theta + (r_0 - \theta)\dfrac{1 - e^{-\kappa T}}{\kappa T}$. The shaded area is the integral.
screens.question: For $T = 5$, what is the average rate, to 4 decimal places of a per cent?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $0.02e^{-0.5t}$ from 0 to 5, divide by 5, add 4%.

byKey.mid: You averaged the start and the mean. The path is curved, so it is closer to 4% for longer.
byKey.end: That is $r(5)$, the rate at the end. The average includes the higher early years.

explain.text: $\int_0^5 0.02e^{-0.5t}dt = 0.04(1 - e^{-2.5}) = 0.036717$; divided by 5 and added to 4% it is 4.7343%. The average sits above $r(5) = 4.1642\%$ because early rates are higher.

screens.title: Adding noise: the Vasicek model
screens.prose: The Vasicek model adds shocks: $dr = \kappa(\theta - r)\,dt + \sigma\,dW$. Daily, it is an AR(1): each day keeps $\phi = e^{-\kappa/252} \approx 0.998018$ of the gap. The shocks have mean zero, so the dashed mean path solves our equation.
screens.question: What is the **expected** rate after 252 trading days, to 4 decimal places of a per cent?

widget.accept: 5.2131%: the noise averages out, so $E[r(1)] = 4\% + 2\% \times e^{-0.5}$

hints.text: Shocks with mean zero do not move the mean.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The noise has mean zero, so the mean path is the solution from screen 2.

byKey.start: You reasoned that noise makes the future unknowable, so the start is the best guess. The drift still pulls the mean down.
byKey.theta: That is where it ends in the long run. After one year the gap is still $0.02e^{-0.5}$.

explain.text: $\phi^{252} = e^{-0.5}$ exactly, so the dashed mean after a year is 5.2131%. Noise spreads the paths around it; `ito` studies that spread. The same AR(1) comes back in `arma` l12 and `coint` l7, later courses.

screens.title: Half of what?
screens.prose: A colleague says: "$\kappa = 0.5$, so the half-life is 1.39 years. The rate will have halved to 3% by then." Another writes the drift as $0.5(r - 0.04)$.
screens.question: Where is the rate after 1.3863 years?

options.why: You halved the rate itself. The half-life halves the gap to $\theta$, from 2 points to 1.
You used the drift $0.5(r - 0.04)$, which pushes away from 4%. The gap then doubles.
The rate gets to 4% only in the long run; one half-life leaves half the gap.

feedback.correct: The gap halves from 2 points to 1, so the rate is 5%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Halve the gap to $\theta$, not the rate.

byKey.three: You halved the rate itself. Mean reversion halves the gap to $\theta$: 6% goes to 5%.
byKey.eight: You used the drift $0.5(r - 0.04)$: above 4% it pushes up, so the gap doubles instead.

explain.text: After one half-life the gap is $2\% \times \tfrac12 = 1\%$, so $r = 5\%$. The drift must be $\kappa(\theta - r)$: with the signs swapped the rate runs away.

screens.title: The mean-reverting solution
screens.prose:
For $\dfrac{dr}{dt} = \kappa(\theta - r)$ with $\kappa > 0$:

$$r(t) = \theta + (r_0 - \theta)e^{-\kappa t}, \qquad t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\kappa}.$$

Every half-life halves the gap. To reach a target $r^*$, solve $e^{-\kappa t} = \dfrac{r^* - \theta}{r_0 - \theta}$.
screens.question: From 6%, how long until the rate reaches 4.5%, in years to 4 decimal places?

feedback.correct: The gap falls from 2 to 0.5, a quarter: two half-lives, $\ln 4/0.5 = 2.7726$ years.

byKey.one: One half-life leaves 1 point, so the rate is 5%. You need a quarter of the gap.
byKey.lin: You kept the starting slope, 1 point a year. The fall slows as the gap shrinks.

explain.text: $(0.045 - 0.04)/(0.06 - 0.04) = \tfrac14$, so $t = \ln 4/0.5 = 2.7726$ years. Two half-lives leave a quarter.

screens.title: The drift in NumPy
screens.prose: Code the mean path, the half-life and the time to a target. Two edge cases: with $\kappa \le 0$ nothing reverts, so there is no half-life. And $\theta$ itself is never reached, only approached.
screens.question: Complete the three functions.

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests. Values are rounded as in the calls and compared within a relative 1e-9. Four cases must raise ValueError. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: Raise when `kappa <= 0`, and when the ratio is not in $(0, 1]$.

feedback.correct: The closed form, its half-life and its inverse, each with its guard.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check the guards: $\kappa \le 0$, and a target that is not strictly between $\theta$ and $r_0$ (or equal to $r_0$).

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace each `...` with code that returns.

explain.text:
The gap ratio must lie in $(0, 1]$: 0 is $\theta$ itself, and above 1 is further away than the start.

```python
ratio = (target - theta) / (r0 - theta)
if not (0 < ratio <= 1):
    raise ValueError("target is not between r0 and theta")
```

screens.title: Calibrating the speed
screens.prose: A rates desk watches the forward rate converge on its long-run level. The gap to $\theta$ falls from 150 basis points to 50 in two years. It fits $\kappa$ and quotes the half-life to traders.
screens.question: What $\kappa$ fits, to 4 decimal places?

hints.text: The gap shrinks by a factor of 3.

feedback.correct: $e^{-2\kappa} = \tfrac13$, so $\kappa = \ln 3/2 = 0.5493$ and the half-life is $\ln 2/0.5493 = 1.26$ years.

byKey.lin: You took the fall, 100 bp in 2 years, as a straight line. The gap decays exponentially.
byKey.ln3: You found $\ln 3$ and stopped. Divide by the 2 years.

explain.text: $\kappa = \ln 3/2 = 0.5493$ a year, a half-life of 1.26 years. A pairs desk does the same for a spread, in days; `coint` l7 returns to it.

ideas: $r' = \kappa(\theta - r)$ pulls the rate to $\theta$: the gap $r - \theta$ decays as $e^{-\kappa t}$.
The half-life $\ln 2/\kappa$ halves the gap, not the rate; two half-lives leave a quarter.
The Vasicek model adds mean-zero noise, so its expected path is exactly this solution.
summary.trap: Halving the rate instead of the gap, or writing the drift as $\kappa(r - \theta)$.

quiz.prose: A rate starts at its long-run mean: $r_0 = \theta = 4\%$, $\kappa = 0.5$.
quiz.question: What is $r(3)$?

feedback.correct: With no gap there is no drift: the rate stays at 4%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the gap at the start.

byKey.half: You halved the rate. With no gap there is nothing to halve.

explain.text: $r_0 - \theta = 0$, so $r(t) = \theta + 0 \cdot e^{-\kappa t} = 4\%$ for every $t$. It is the equilibrium of the drift.

quiz.question: What does the mean path do from $r_0 = 6\%$ with $\theta = 4\%$?

options.text: The gap grows as $e^{0.2t}$, so there is no half-life

options.why: A negative $\kappa$ flips the drift: the gap grows instead.
That is $\kappa = 0$. Here the drift is $-0.2(0.04 - r) > 0$ above 4%.
Nothing in the equation jumps; it moves away from 4% smoothly.

feedback.correct: $e^{-\kappa t} = e^{0.2t}$ grows: the rate moves away from $\theta$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $\kappa = -0.2$ into $e^{-\kappa t}$.

explain.text: With $\kappa < 0$ the gap is multiplied by $e^{0.2t}$, so it doubles every 3.47 years. There is no reversion and no half-life.

quiz.prose: A spread reverts with $\kappa = 2$ a year.
quiz.question: What is its half-life in years, to 4 decimal places?

byKey.recip: You took $1/\kappa$. The half-life needs the $\ln 2$.
byKey.times: You multiplied by $\kappa$ instead of dividing.

quiz.question: Where is it after two half-lives?

widget.accept: 5%: a quarter of the 4-point gap is left

feedback.correct: Two half-lives leave $\tfrac14$ of the gap: 1 point, so 5%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Halve the 4-point gap twice.

byKey.two: You halved the rate twice. It is the gap that halves.

explain.text: The gap goes 4, 2, 1 points, so the rate is $4\% + 1\% = 5\%$.
